lines.text: You tap the faun on the shoulder. She jumps, notices her wet hoof, and turns the flute off.
"Wagons,"
she whispers.
"Rush wagons, heading for the pumpkins."
Then, because you asked so nicely, she pulls a spare reed whistle out of her hat.
"For when you need everybody to hear you. Just one loud note, though. It only has the one."
Rush wagons are cutting through the unpicked pumpkins to dodge a jam. A faun foreman named Hob Thistledown waves his hat.
"Help me turn them, before the whole season is soup!"
The wagons take the edge track. Hob starts the song again with your names in it and hands out honeycake.
"Crowded all the way to Bramblewood now,"
he says.
Hob tells you the life story of every pumpkin. The biggest one is called Gerald. At the crossroads he sniffs.
"Eggs. Whatever rush folk pay, neighbors should not have to."
You sing the verse back, names and all, and get the tune wrong twice. Hob is delighted anyway.
"Now you're Sunward,"
he says.
"Any faun who hears that verse will help you."
At the crossroads, a faun egg seller chalks higher prices for the rush.
"Rush folk pay rush prices!"
she laughs. At the back, a faun dad counts too few coins. Her hen looks offended.
The egg seller laughs so hard she sits down on the cart.
"I can't do sums either!"
She sells the faun dad his eggs at last year's price, then charges the next rude wagon double. The hen approves.
The kitsune hops on the cart.
"The line starts here!"
Rush folk cannot resist a line. Twelve buyers join it without knowing why. By the time they reach the front, the faun dad has his eggs at the old price.
About thirty sheeple stand in one woolly knot, all in the same seven-brimmed hat.
"What do we think?"
asks the middle one.
"We think wolves,"
they answer, out of step.
"In the grass."
"We all saw them."
"Because one of us did."
The bigfoot steps into the canal and lifts the cracked plank on their shoulders.
"Go on,"
they say. Cart after cart rolls over. The duck sits on the bigfoot's head like a hat.
"That's impossible,"
says the dragonling.
"Embermoths fly toward warm. Always. Back home the grandmothers would be ringing the bells."
Nobody laughs. A little moth lands on the dragonling's horn, as if to say: tell them again.
The cook snores like a kettle, then like two kettles. The ground gives one more tiny shiver.
"Pass the gravy,"
says the cook, fast asleep. You give up and go to sleep too.
"The bridge ones!"
Tiny trumpets play. The sprites offer a bench much too small for you, then proudly show you what they guard.
In the middle of the row sits a green-gold sky-stone wearing a woven BEST medal.
"It fell here, so it belongs here,"
the sprites say. You could trade, earn it, leave it, or take it anyway. They will remember.
There is an award ceremony. The best beet gets a medal. The best bean gets a medal. Then the sprites hand you the Harvest Stone, medal and all.
"Keep it somewhere with a nice view."
The egg cart rattles up, and the egg seller waves you aboard.
"Neighbor price. Free!"
She takes a farm lane the rush has never heard of, with the hen on your lap, and drops you at the hedges.
Outside Bramblewood's tall hedges, a mob of treasure hunters shouts, "Open up!" The hedges ignore them. A small thorny sprite with a huge satchel trims one leaf at a time.
"I'm Pib. I keep the hedges. They only open for people who ask properly. Will you?"
You bow to the hedge. The three sheeple who followed you bow too, then call in silence. Soon thirty sheeple arrive, bowing.
"Please may we come in?"
they say, out of step. The mob goes quiet. The hedge opens a path wide enough for {party}, and the flock trots in too.
Pib sees the sprites' medal and gasps.
"You've met my cousins!"
The hedge opens before Pib finishes the sentence. A thorn reaches out and gently straightens the little medal.
Inside, Pib walks you up the lane to an inn with very tall doors, then digs in the satchel.
"I can only spare one gift for you,"
says Pib.
"The hedge says you should choose it together."
Which one? Everybody vote.
Pib pins the thistle on your coat.
"Prickly,"
they say.
"But only on the outside. Like a hedge."
The thistle stands up very straight, proud to be chosen.
Pib hands over a soft gray owl feather on a clasp.
"The hedge kept it for somebody clever. It thinks that might be you. It isn't sure."
The feather tickles, as if it is still thinking.
Pib drops a pebble with a hole in it into your hand.
"When things go wrong, look through the hole, and they go a bit less wrong."
Pib shows you, staring through it for a very long time.
A centaur innkeeper named Marda Thorn ducks under her own huge door and brings you stew.
"Eat first,"
she says.
"There is time."
Three tables argue about the roads north. A rumor board waits under a lamp.
Marda holds the warm red stone to her ear. The room goes quiet. The stone hums.
"Mm,"
says Marda, and wipes her hand on her apron, as if the hum might rub off. Then she asks her question.
Marda pulls up a stool, which creaks.
"I ask everybody this season: where is it all going?"
She doesn't mean the road. She waits for your whole answer.
"Me, I believe all three rumors. That's the trouble."
You can only hear one table properly. A frogfolk ferrier sits by the window. A muddy relay runner sits by the fire. A rush drover eats three dinners by the door.
"Whose news will you hear?"
asks Marda.
The ferrier talks slowly. West, the Whispering Marsh is busy for the first time in a hundred years. Her cousins pole travelers they like. Rude ones get left on an island to think.
"If the marsh likes you, it's the gentlest road."
The runner talks fast. East, the line at Stone Crossing is moving again. The trolls there take a story instead of coins. A river drake charges double if you won't wait.
"Past the river, you see trouble coming a day away."
The drover talks with her mouth full. North is the shortest road, and the whole rush is on it, wheel to wheel.
"You don't walk the Rush Road,"
she says.
"You fall in, and it carries you to the ford. Then you wait."
The rumor board shows three roads north. East, the River Road to Stone Crossing. North, the Rush Road, with everybody else. West, the Wild Road through the marsh.
"Shorter is not quicker,"
says Marda. Which road?
You pass the egg baskets down the line while the hen watches every shell. Not one cracks. The egg seller tucks a wrapped supper into your pack.
"For the road,"
she says.
A long gray plank lies across the last ditch. A faun called Burdock twists his hat.
"Don't step on it,"
he whispers.
"It's a mire mimic, mud pretending to be a plank. My hay needs to cross!"
The plank blinks. So does a smaller one beside it.
The planks go floppy and slide away down the ditch. Underneath is a heap of things the rush dropped: four coins and a drover's brave whistle.
"Finders keepers,"
says Burdock.
"Thank you!"
The hay cart rolls over on good solid mud. On the far side, Burdock's wife has a table of warm honeycakes.
"Two coins a cake,"
she says.
"Or a thank-you, which is also nice."
Near the hedges, a wagon wheel is stuck deep in a rut. Its drover, a very polite centaur, waves you over.
"Wait for my pull, then push,"
she says.
"I tip well."
With a slurp, the wheel pops free. The drover counts three coins into your hand.
"Told you."
You push a heartbeat too early. The wheel slides back in with a squelch, then pops out by itself.
"Next time I'll ask the oxen,"
says the drover, and trots off without a coin for anyone.
The fauns from the canal bridge catch up with their long brace pole.
"You helped our bridge,"
they say. One branch is tangled. Hold the brace where the branch can slip free.
You count it out for Marda: the moths, the wolves, the watching jackalopes, the shiver. She stops wiping the table.
"So the fields have noticed too,"
she says. She sets down an extra bowl of stew, then presses three coins into your hand.
"For saying it out loud. Go carefully, whichever road you pick."
You count the moths, the wolves and the shiver on your fingers and ask Marda what it adds up to. She stops wiping the table.
"Everything that can leave Mount Red Sky is leaving it,"
she says.
"The fields noticed before I did. Go carefully, whichever road you pick."
